Moonquakes do occur on the Moon, but the extent to which they resemble earthquakes on Earth is a matter of differing scientific perspectives. According to the USGS [d3], moonquakes "do occur, but they happen less frequently and have smaller magnitudes than earthquakes on the Earth," and appear related to tidal stresses rather than plate tectonics. Some sources describe moonquakes as "similar to earthquakes on Earth" [d10], with at least four types and some registering up to 5.5 on the Richter scale, while Wikipedia [d2] calls a moonquake "the lunar equivalent of an earthquake" but notes they "are caused in different ways" and can last up to an hour. In contrast, d4 and d7 emphasize fundamental differences: the Moon lacks tectonic plates, so it "doesn't experience quakes when tectonic plates move into or past each other the way Earth does" [d4], and the total annual energy released by moonquakes (~10¹² J) is roughly a million times less than that of earthquakes (~10¹⁸ J) [d7]. Scientific American [d12] notes that shallow moonquakes are "more like those we experience on Earth," while deep moonquakes result from interior heat loss and contraction rather than plate collision, and d9 highlights that moonquakes resonate far longer on the dry, rigid Moon—often ten minutes or more—unlike earthquakes, which typically cease within a few minutes.
